title: Optimal Approximations for the Requirement Cut Problem on Sparse Graph Classes
summary:
We study the Requirement Cut problem, a generalization of numerous classical
graph partitioning problems including Multicut, Multiway Cut, $k$-Cut, and
Steiner Multicut among others. Given a graph with edge costs, terminal groups
$(S_1, ..., S_g)$ and integer requirements $(r_1,... , r_g)$; the goal is to
compute a minimum-cost edge cut that separates each group $S_i$ into at least
$r_i$ connected components. Despite many efforts, the best known approximation
for Requirement Cut yields a double-logarithmic $O(\log(g).\log(n))$
approximation ratio as it relies on embedding general graphs into trees and
solving the tree instance.
  In this paper, we explore two largely unstudied structural parameters in
order to obtain single-logarithmic approximation ratios: (1) the number of
minimal Steiner trees in the instance, which in particular is upper-bounded by
the number of spanning trees of the graphs multiplied by $g$, and (2) the depth
of series-parallel graphs. Specifically, we show that if the number of minimal
Steiner trees is polynomial in $n$, then a simple LP-rounding algorithm yields
an $O(\log n)$-approximation, and if the graph is series-parallel with a
constant depth then a refined analysis of a known probabilistic embedding
yields a $O(depth.\log(g))$-approximation on series-parallel graphs of bounded
depth. Both results extend the known class of graphs that have a
single-logarithmic approximation ratio.

bib.abstract:
We investigate recursive relations for the Grothendieck classes of the affine graph hypersurface complements of melonic graphs. We compute these classes explicitly for several families of melonic graphs, focusing on the case of graphs with valence-

4

internal vertices, relevant to CTKT tensor models. The results hint at a complex and interesting structure in terms of divisibility relations or nontrivial relations between classes of graphs in different families. Using the recursive relations, we prove that the Grothendieck classes of all melonic graphs are positive as polynomials in the class of the moduli space

{\textbackslash}mathcal M\_\{0,4\}

. We also conjecture that the corresponding polynomials are
log-concave
, on the basis of hundreds of explicit computations.
bib.title: Motives of melonic graphs

bib.abstract: The k-cut problem is to find a partition of an edge weighted graph into k nonempty components, such that the total edge weight between components is minimum. bib.abstract: We introduce and study l\_p-norm-multiway-cut: the input here is an undirected graph with non-negative edge weights along with k terminals and the goal is to find a partition of the vertex set into k parts each containing exactly one terminal so as to minimize the l\_p-norm of the cut values of the parts. This is a unified generalization of min-sum multiway cut (when p = 1) and min-max multiway cut (when p = ∞), both of which are well-studied classic problems in the graph partitioning literature. We show that l\_p-norm-multiway-cut is NP-hard for constant number of terminals and is NP-hard in planar graphs. On the algorithmic side, we design an O(log² n)-approximation for all p ≥ 1. We also show an integrality gap of Ω(k{\textasciicircum}\{1-1/p\}) for a natural convex program and an O(k{\textasciicircum}\{1-1/p-ε\})-inapproximability for any constant ε {\textgreater} 0 assuming the small set expansion hypothesis.

bib.abstract:
In an undirected graph, a k-cut is a set of edges whose removal breaks the graph into at least k connected components. The minimum weight k-cut can be computed in n{\textasciicircum}O(k) time, but when k is treated as part of the input, computing the minimum weight k-cut is NP-Hard [Goldschmidt and Hochbaum, 1994]. For poly(m,n,k)-time algorithms, the best possible approximation factor is essentially 2 under the small set expansion hypothesis [Manurangsi, 2017]. Saran and Vazirani [1995] showed that a (2 - 2/k)-approximately minimum weight k-cut can be computed via O(k) minimum cuts, which implies a O{\textasciitilde}(km) randomized running time via the nearly linear time randomized min-cut algorithm of Karger [2000]. Nagamochi and Kamidoi [2007] showed that a (2 - 2/k)-approximately minimum weight k-cut can be computed deterministically in O(mn + n{\textasciicircum}2 log n) time. These results prompt two basic questions. The first concerns the role of randomization. Is there a deterministic algorithm for 2-approximate k-cuts matching the randomized running time of O{\textasciitilde}(km)? The second question qualitatively compares minimum cut to 2-approximate minimum k-cut. Can 2-approximate k-cuts be computed as fast as the minimum cut - in O{\textasciitilde}(m) randomized time? 
We give a deterministic approximation algorithm that computes (2 + eps)-minimum k-cuts in O(m log{\textasciicircum}3 n / eps{\textasciicircum}2) time, via a (1 + eps)-approximation for an LP relaxation of k-cut.

bib.abstract: In the k-cut problem, we want to find the lowest-weight set of edges whose deletion breaks a given (multi)graph into k connected components. Algorithms of Karger and Stein can solve this in roughly O(n2k) time. However, lower bounds from conjectures about the k-clique problem imply that Ω (n(1-o(1))k) time is likely needed. Recent results of Gupta, Lee, and Li have given new algorithms for general k-cut in n1.98k + O(1) time, as well as specialized algorithms with better performance for certain classes of graphs (e.g., for small integer edge weights).In this work, we resolve the problem for general graphs. We show that the Contraction Algorithm of Karger outputs any fixed k-cut of weight α λ k with probability Ωk(n-α k), where λ k denotes the minimum k-cut weight. This also gives an extremal bound of Ok(nk) on the number of minimum k-cuts and an algorithm to compute λ k with roughly nk polylog(n) runtime. Both are tight up to lower-order factors, with the algorithmic lower bound assuming hardness of max-weight k-clique.The first main ingredient in our result is an extremal bound on the number of cuts of weight less than 2 λk/k, using the Sunflower lemma. The second ingredient is a fine-grained analysis of how the graph shrinks—and how the average degree evolves—in the Karger process.
bib.title: Optimal {Bounds} for the k-cut {Problem}

bib.abstract:
We consider variants of the classic Multiway Cut problem. Multiway Cut asks to partition a graph G into k parts so as to separate k given terminals. Recently, Chandrasekaran and Wang (ESA 2021) introduced 𝓁\_p-norm Multiway Cut, a generalization of the problem, in which the goal is to minimize the 𝓁\_p norm of the edge boundaries of k parts. We provide an O(log{\textasciicircum}\{1/2\} nlog{\textasciicircum}\{1/2+1/p\} k) approximation algorithm for this problem, improving upon the approximation guarantee of O(log{\textasciicircum}\{3/2\} n log{\textasciicircum}\{1/2\} k) due to Chandrasekaran and Wang. 
We also introduce and study Norm Multiway Cut, a further generalization of Multiway Cut. We assume that we are given access to an oracle, which answers certain queries about the norm. We present an O(log{\textasciicircum}\{1/2\} n log{\textasciicircum}\{7/2\} k) approximation algorithm with a weaker oracle and an O(log{\textasciicircum}\{1/2\} n log{\textasciicircum}\{5/2\} k) approximation algorithm with a stronger oracle. Additionally, we show that without any oracle access, there is no n{\textasciicircum}\{1/4-ε\} approximation algorithm for every ε {\textgreater} 0 assuming the Hypergraph Dense-vs-Random Conjecture.

bib.abstract: We consider the Steiner Multicut problem, which asks, given an undirected graph G, a collection T=\{T1,…,Tt\}, Ti⊆V(G), of terminal sets of size at most p, and an integer k, whether there is a set S of at most k edges or nodes such that of each set Ti at least one pair of terminals is in different connected components of G−S. We provide a dichotomy of the parameterized complexity of Steiner Multicut. For any combination of k, t, p, and the treewidth tw(G) as constant, parameter, or unbounded, and for all versions of the problem (edge deletion and node deletion with and without deletable terminals), we prove either that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable, W[1]-hard, or (para-)NP-complete. Our characterization includes a dichotomy for Steiner Multicut on trees as well as a polynomial time versus NP-hardness dichotomy (by restricting k,t,p,tw(G) to constant or unbounded).
bib.title: Parameterized complexity dichotomy for {Steiner} {Multicut}

title: NetPress: Dynamically Generated LLM Benchmarks for Network Applications
summary:
Despite growing interest in domain-specific benchmarking of large language
models (LLMs) and agents, current evaluations remain limited to static,
small-scale datasets, especially in high-stakes tasks like network operations
that demand reliability for deployments. We present NetPress, an automated
benchmark generation framework for evaluating LLM agents in network
applications. NetPress introduces a unified abstraction with state and action,
enabling dynamic generation of diverse query sets along with corresponding
ground truths. At runtime, users can specify benchmark configurations to
generate millions of queries on the fly. In addition to dynamic benchmark
construction, NetPress integrates with network emulators to provide realistic
environment feedback, supporting comprehensive evaluation across correctness,
safety, and latency. We instantiate NetPress on three representative
applications, revealing interesting fine-grained differences in agent behavior
that static, correctness-only benchmarks often miss. NetPress moves LLM
evaluation toward realistic, scalable testing in infrastructure-centric
domains, helping close the gap between benchmark performance and real-world
deployment readiness. Code is available at
https://github.com/Froot-NetSys/NetPress.

title: Data-Informed Mathematical Characterization of Absorption Properties in Artificial and Natural Porous Materials
summary:
In this work, we characterize the water absorption properties of selected
porous materials through a combined approach that integrates laboratory
experiments and mathematical modeling. Specifically, experimental data from
imbibition tests on marble, travertine, wackestone and mortar mock-ups are used
to inform and validate the mathematical and simulation frameworks. First, a
monotonicity-preserving fitting procedure is developed to preprocess the
measurements, aiming to reduce noise and mitigate instrumental errors. The
imbibition process is then simulated through a partial differential equation
model, with parameters calibrated against rough and smoothed data. The proposed
procedure appears particularly effective to characterize absorption properties
of different materials and it represents a reliable tool for the study and
preservation of cultural heritage.

title: Diffusion-based Task-oriented Semantic Communications with Model Inversion Attack
summary:
Semantic communication has emerged as a promising neural network-based system
design for 6G networks. Task-oriented semantic communication is a novel
paradigm whose core goal is to efficiently complete specific tasks by
transmitting semantic information, optimizing communication efficiency and task
performance. The key challenge lies in preserving privacy while maintaining
task accuracy, as this scenario is susceptible to model inversion attacks. In
such attacks, adversaries can restore or even reconstruct input data by
analyzing and processing model outputs, owing to the neural network-based
nature of the systems. In addition, traditional systems use image quality
indicators (such as PSNR or SSIM) to assess attack severity, which may be
inadequate for task-oriented semantic communication, since visual differences
do not necessarily ensure semantic divergence. In this paper, we propose a
diffusion-based semantic communication framework, named DiffSem, that optimizes
semantic information reconstruction through a diffusion mechanism with
self-referential label embedding to significantly improve task performance. Our
model also compensates channel noise and adopt semantic information distortion
to ensure the robustness of the system in various signal-to-noise ratio
environments. To evaluate the attacker's effectiveness, we propose a new metric
that better quantifies the semantic fidelity of estimations from the adversary.
Experimental results based on this criterion show that on the MNIST dataset,
DiffSem improves the classification accuracy by 10.03%, and maintain stable
performance under dynamic channels. Our results further demonstrate that
significant deviation exists between traditional image quality indicators and
the leakage of task-relevant semantic information.

title: Emerging Media Use and Acceptance of Digital Immortality: A Cluster Analysis among Chinese Young Generations
summary:
The rapid technological advancements made the concept of digital immortality
less fantastical and more plausible, sparking academic and industrial interest.
Existing literature mainly discusses philosophical and societal aspects,
lacking specific empirical observation. To address this gap, we conducted a
study among Chinese youth to gauge their acceptance of digital immortality.
Using cluster analysis, we classified participants into three groups: "geeks,"
"video game players," and "laggards" based on their media usage. Those most
receptive to digital immortality, termed "geeks" tend to be male, with higher
income levels, openness, conscientiousness, extensive engagement with emerging
media technology, and surprisingly, more adhering to Buddhism and Daoism.
Overall, this study examined media usage patterns and youth perspectives on
digital immortality, shedding light on technology's role in shaping views on
life and death. It highlights the importance of further research on the
profound implications of digital immortality in the context of contemporary
society.

title: From Coarse to Fine-Grained Emotion Annotation: An Immediate Recall Paradigm with Validation through Physiological Evidence and Recognition Performance
summary:
Traditional video-induced emotion physiological datasets often use
whole-trial annotation, assigning a single emotion label to all data collected
during an entire trial. This coarse-grained annotation approach misaligns with
the dynamic and temporally localized nature of emotional responses as they
unfold with video narratives, introducing label noise that limits emotion
recognition algorithm evaluation and performance. To solve the label noise
problem caused by coarse-grained annotation, we propose a fine-grained
annotation method through an immediate recall paradigm. This paradigm
integrates an immediate video replay phase after the initial stimulus viewing,
allowing participants to precisely mark the onset timestamp, emotion label, and
intensity based on their immediate recall. We validate this paradigm through
physiological evidence and recognition performance. Physiological validation of
multimodal signals within participant-marked windows revealed rhythm-specific
EEG patterns and arousal-dependent GSR responses-with SCRs appearing in 91% of
high-arousal versus 6% of low-arousal emotion windows. These objective
physiological data changes strongly aligned with subjective annotations,
confirming annotation precision. For recognition performance, classification
experiments showed that models trained on fine-grained annotations achieved
9.7% higher accuracy than traditional whole-trial labeling, despite using less
data. This work not only addresses label noise through fine-grained annotation
but also demonstrates that annotation precision outweighs data scale in
determining emotion recognition performance.

\begin{abstract}

Traditional video-induced emotion physiological datasets often use whole-trial annotation, assigning a single emotion label to all data collected during an entire trial. This coarse-grained annotation approach misaligns with the dynamic and temporally localized nature of emotional responses as they unfold with video narratives, introducing label noise that limits emotion recognition algorithm evaluation and performance. To solve the label noise problem caused by coarse-grained annotation, we propose a fine-grained annotation method through an immediate recall paradigm. This paradigm integrates an immediate video replay phase after the initial stimulus viewing, allowing participants to precisely mark the onset timestamp, emotion label, and intensity based on their immediate recall. We validate this paradigm through physiological evidence and recognition performance. Physiological validation of multimodal signals within participant-marked windows revealed rhythm-specific EEG patterns and arousal-dependent GSR responses—with SCRs appearing in 91\% of high-arousal versus 6\% of low-arousal emotion windows. These objective physiological data changes strongly aligned with subjective annotations, confirming annotation precision. For recognition performance, classification experiments showed that models trained on fine-grained annotations achieved 9.7\% higher accuracy than traditional whole-trial labeling, despite using less data. This work not only addresses label noise through fine-grained annotation but also demonstrates that annotation precision outweighs data scale in determining emotion recognition performance.

\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Emotion Annotation, Label Noise, Multimodal Emotion Dataset, Physiological Validation, Emotion Recognition.
\end{IEEEkeywords}


\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{E}{motion} is a subjective experience elicited by external stimuli \cite{frijda2005emotion}, typically accompanied by physiological responses and behavioral tendencies. Emotions play a crucial role in individual survival, social interaction \cite{lopes2005emotion}, and decision-making processes \cite{rolls2014emotion}. Two primary theoretical frameworks describe emotions: discrete and dimensional models. The discrete model, exemplified by Ekman's seminal work \cite{ekman1999basic}, identifies six basic emotions—happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust—each linked to specific neural circuits. For instance, fear demonstrates strong associations with amygdala activation. In contrast, the dimensional model, represented by Russell's Circumplex Model \cite{russell1980circumplex}, characterizes emotions along two dimensions: valence and arousal. These complementary frameworks establish a robust theoretical foundation for emotion research.

To explore neural mechanisms and develop recognition methods for emotions, researchers have designed various experimental paradigms to simulate and capture human emotional responses. These experiments typically employ music \cite{eerola2012review}, images \cite{junghofer2001fleeting}, or videos \cite{soleymani2011multimodal} as stimuli while collecting participants' physiological and behavioral signals. Among these modalities, video stimuli demonstrate superior performance in eliciting complex emotions due to their dynamic nature and multisensory input, thereby offering higher ecological validity compared to static images or single-modality audio stimuli \cite{siedlecka2019experimental}. Data collection encompasses both physiological signals (e.g., electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG)) \cite{alarcao2017emotions,hsu2017automatic} and non-physiological signals (e.g., facial expressions) \cite{liu2017facial}, providing comprehensive documentation of emotional manifestations. Physiological signals offer high temporal resolution and objectivity, enabling precise capture of neural and physiological changes associated with emotions \cite{shu2018review}. Non-physiological signals provide behavioral cues that complement physiological measures, further deepening our multidimensional understanding of emotional mechanisms \cite{pillalamarri2025review}.

Despite continuous developments in experimental paradigms for emotion research, existing methods face significant challenges in emotion annotation accuracy. Datasets such as SEED \cite{zheng2015investigating} and DEAP \cite{koelstra2011deap} employ coarse-grained annotation strategies, assigning single emotion labels to entire multi-minute trials. While this approach reduces annotation time, it overlooks the temporal instability and discrete nature of emotions, resulting in substantial label noise. To address this limitation, Zhang et al. \cite{zhang2022eeg} proposed an emotion localization task for the SEED dataset. They segmented each video stimulus into multiple intervals and recruited 20 annotators to evaluate whether each segment triggered the target emotion. Segments receiving majority agreement were labeled as ground truth, thereby reducing noise by focusing on highly relevant emotional segments. Building upon this foundation \cite{zhang2022eeg}, Zhang et al. \cite{zhang2023unsupervised} introduced TAS-Net, an unsupervised time-aware sampling network based on deep reinforcement learning. This approach automatically detects key emotional segments in EEG signals while reducing labeling noise from traditional fixed-label methods. The method's accuracy was validated by comparing detected segments with manually re-annotated segments. Similarly, Jiang et al. proposed REMONET \cite{jiang2024remonet}, which mitigates sentiment label noise through a multi-regularization co-learning framework that coordinates different self-supervised data views to prevent model overfitting to noisy labels. However, these post-hoc approaches—whether through manual re-annotation or deep learning techniques—do not fundamentally resolve the inherent ambiguity in mapping physiological data to subjective emotion labels \cite{winter1997individual}.

In recent efforts to address annotation granularity, researchers have developed multimodal datasets such as SEED-VII \cite{jiang2024seed} and MGEED \cite{wang2023mgeed}, aiming to achieve finer-grained emotional labeling. SEED-VII represents a significant advancement by incorporating both trial-by-trial intensity ratings and post-session continuous annotation. Specifically, participants provide immediate intensity feedback after each trial, then retrospectively assign frame-level emotional intensities while reviewing all videos at the session's conclusion. This dual-annotation approach attempts to capture both immediate impressions and detailed temporal dynamics. Similarly, MGEED employs a comprehensive frame-by-frame retrospective protocol, where participants meticulously annotate their emotional states for each video frame after viewing all experimental stimuli. While these methodologies achieve fine-grained temporal annotation, both datasets fundamentally rely on delayed recall mechanisms. This ``watch first, annotate later'' paradigm, despite its temporal granularity, introduces significant cognitive load \cite{barrouillet2007time}, as participants must accurately remember and differentiate emotional experiences across multiple stimuli viewed over extended periods. Moreover, inherent memory bias \cite{thomas1990memory} in delayed reporting may lead to temporal displacement of emotional events or conflation of distinct emotional episodes, potentially compromising annotation reliability.

To achieve fine-grained emotion annotation while mitigating memory bias, we propose an immediate recall annotation paradigm and establish the Fine-grained Immediate Recall-based Multimodal Emotion Dataset (\textbf{FIRMED}). This approach introduces three key methodological advancements:

\textbf{1) Precise Temporal Localization via Immediate Recall:} To achieve precise temporal localization of emotional events within each trial, our paradigm incorporates an immediate replay phase following stimulus presentation. During post-stimulus replay, participants retrospectively identify and mark the discrete time point $t_{\text{event}}$ at which they recall first experiencing the target emotion during initial viewing. A fixed-duration window (4 seconds) centered at $t_{\text{event}}$ is then extracted for analysis, associating data within this window with the reported emotion label and intensity. This recall-based discrete annotation during immediate replay aims to overcome temporal ambiguity in whole-trial labeling while reducing memory decay biases associated with delayed annotation protocols.

\textbf{2) Expanded Multimodal Data for Enhanced Reliability:} To improve annotation reliability and objectivity, we expanded the range of collected physiological signals to include EEG, ECG, galvanic skin response (GSR), and photoplethysmogram (PPG) data. Additionally, we captured participants' facial expressions via camera during stimulus viewing, providing behavioral data on emotional responses. This multimodal collection strategy enriches data variety and enables cross-validation of subjective annotations using various physiological data.

\textbf{3) Ecologically Valid Stimuli:} We extensively utilize short videos from social media platforms as stimuli, encompassing authentic scenes including daily life recordings and news reports. Compared to traditional movie clips or music videos, these stimuli more accurately reflect natural emotional experiences, offering enhanced ecological validity. Participant feedback regarding stimulus effectiveness further supports this choice.

To validate this paradigm's effectiveness, we conducted systematic physiological and computational analyses. Physiologically, by analyzing multimodal signals within precisely annotated windows, we found strong evidence of both central \cite{hagemann2003central} and autonomic nervous system engagement \cite{kreibig2010autonomic}. This included discovering emotion-specific spectral patterns in EEG signals and strong temporal coupling between discrete annotations and objective autonomic nervous system activation markers, exemplified by specific skin conductance response (SCR) patterns reliably occurring for high-arousal emotions \cite{xia2017salience}. Computationally, emotion classification experiments compared the effectiveness of the two labeling strategies. Results demonstrate that standard classifiers trained using precise labels from FIRMED significantly outperform identical models trained using traditional whole-trial labels applied to corresponding full trial segments from the same data, thereby quantifying the positive impact of reduced label noise on recognition performance.



\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Evolution of Physiological Signal-Based Emotion Datasets}

Video-based emotion elicitation has established itself as the predominant stimulus modality for inducing emotional responses in controlled experimental environments, driving the proliferation of multimodal datasets across the affective computing domain \cite{li2022eeg}. These datasets systematically collect multiple physiological signals to provide comprehensive documentation of participants' emotional states \cite{wang2023unlocking}.


Early and highly influential datasets, including DEAP \cite{koelstra2011deap} and the foundational SEED series \cite{zheng2015investigating,zheng2018emotionmeter,liu2021comparing}, established the methodological foundation for physiological emotion analysis through rich signal acquisition protocols. These seminal works adopted a standardized experimental paradigm involving presentation of emotionally evocative stimuli—typically music videos or film clips—followed by collection of self-reported emotional assessments. However, these datasets universally employ whole-trial labeling, wherein single emotion labels are assigned to complete multi-minute stimulus segments.

This coarse-grained annotation strategy ignored the inherently dynamic nature of video stimuli. Emotional responses are characteristically triggered by specific narrative elements—including pivotal plot developments, climactic sequences, or sudden scene transitions—rather than being uniformly sustained throughout extended video segments \cite{hakim2013computational}. Consequently, this labeling granularity introduces label noise \cite{jiang2024remonet}, as temporal segments that fail to elicit the target emotion become erroneously associated with that emotional state.

In direct response to these temporal granularity limitations, recent dataset development efforts have pursued increasingly sophisticated annotation methodologies. The SEED-VII dataset \cite{jiang2024seed} introduced a delayed continuous rating paradigm representing a significant methodological advancement. In this approach, participants retrospectively review all trial videos upon session completion and provide continuous intensity annotations. Similarly, the MGEED database \cite{wang2023mgeed} implemented a delayed frame-by-frame self-assessment protocol, requiring participants to annotate their emotional states retrospectively following complete viewing session.

To systematically characterize these dataset developments, Table \ref{tab:emotion_datasets_comparison} provides a comprehensive comparison of  representative emotion datasets. The analysis reveals a clear evolutionary trajectory from coarse whole-trial labeling toward increasingly fine-grained temporal annotations.

\subsection{Challenges of Emotion Annotation}

The systematic adoption of whole-trial labeling across early multimodal emotion datasets \cite{koelstra2011deap,zheng2015investigating,miranda2018amigos,katsigiannis2017dreamer,soleymani2011multimodal,song2019mped}. This annotation approach suffers from temporal imprecision: emotions constitute dynamic phenomena that evolve synchronously with video narratives \cite{hakim2013computational}, exhibiting rapid fluctuations and transitions rather than maintaining static states across extended durations. The assignment of uniform labels to multi-minute segments obscures emotional transitions and fluctuations \cite{verduyn2015determinants}, causing label noise to be structurally embedded in the dataset. 

While recent datasets such as SEED-VII and MGEED have achieved significant improvements in labeling granularity through delayed recall paradigms. These approaches require participants to complete entire experimental sessions—encompassing numerous stimuli viewed over extended periods (typically 30 minutes to over 1 hour)—before retrospectively annotating their emotional states across all preceding trials. This delayed annotation strategy, despite achieving fine temporal granularity, it also increases the risk of memory bias, which may reduce the reliability of annotations. Cognitive psychology research \cite{colombo2020affect} demonstrates that episodic memory for specific emotional events and their nuanced temporal characteristics becomes increasingly unreliable when recall is required after extended delays involving multiple distinct experiences. 

The persistence of these limitations—temporal imprecision in whole-trial labeling and memory bias in delayed fine-grained annotation—underscores the urgent need for innovative annotation paradigms capable of achieving fine temporal granularity while maintaining annotation reliability.

\section{Experimental Setup}\label{section:sec3}
This Section details the experimental setup and methodology employed in this study during the data collection and preparation stages. The content is divided into four subsections: Section \ref{section:sec3.1} describes the stimuli used for emotion elicitation, Section \ref{section:sec3.2} details the participant demographics and recruitment information, Section \ref{section:sec3.3} elaborates on the complete experimental procedure including the annotation process, and Section \ref{section:sec3.4} explains the data preprocessing steps applied to the acquired multimodal signals.


\subsection{Stimuli}\label{section:sec3.1}
To enhance ecological validity and elicit emotional responses more representative of real-world experiences, we primarily selected short videos sourced from social media platforms (e.g., Douyin, Bilibili, YouTube) as stimuli, each lasting approximately one minute. These videos were often user-generated or edited by creators. The content primarily included daily life recordings and news reports, and the videos typically contained multiple segments potentially capable of evoking specific emotions within the short timeframe.

The stimulus selection involved a rigorous screening process. First, a large pool of candidate videos was initially collected and downloaded from various online platforms by two members of the research team. Subsequently, these candidates were strictly evaluated by a panel of three independent raters who are psychology graduate students trained in emotion recognition. The selection criterion was: only videos for which all three raters unanimously agreed could effectively elicit one specific target basic emotion (Happiness, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Disgust, or Surprise) were ultimately chosen. Videos failing to reach unanimous agreement on a single target emotion or eliciting mixed emotions were excluded during this phase.

Through this rigorous screening process, we obtained the final stimulus set containing 90 selected videos. This set was balanced across the six basic emotions and these 90 videos were evenly distributed across 3 experimental sessions. Each session included 30 trials, with each trial featuring one video specifically selected to elicit one of the six target basic emotions, resulting in 5 distinct videos per emotion category per session. This stimulus selection strategy, prioritizing ecological validity and confirming elicitation of specific target emotions via consensus rating, was corroborated by informal post-experimental feedback from participants; they generally reported that these real-world clips were more engaging and significantly more effective in eliciting their emotional resonance compared to more traditional laboratory stimuli such as movie clips or music videos.

\subsection{Participants}\label{section:sec3.2}
A total of twenty healthy participants (12 males, 8 females) were recruited for this study. Their ages ranged from 22 to 30 years, with a mean age of 24.7 years ± 2.1 years (Mean ± SD). All participants reported being right-handed, having normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders. This study received ethical approval from the Northwestern Polytechnical University Ethics Committee. Before the experiment, the procedure and purpose of the study were introduced to the participants. Subsequently, by signing a consent agreement, participants agreed to the recording, sharing, and publication of their physiological signals and facial images for academic purposes. Participants were aware that their participation was voluntary and that they were free to withdraw at any time without providing any reason. 

\subsection{Protocol}\label{section:sec3.3}
Participants were comfortably seated in a quiet shielded room, at a distance of approximately 70 cm from the display monitor. After providing informed consent and receiving detailed instructions about the task, multimodal physiological sensors including an EEG cap (acquiring 59 channel signals at 1000 Hz), ECG electrodes (acquiring 3 channel signals at 1000 Hz), GSR sensors (acquiring 2 channel signals at 100 Hz), and a PPG sensor (acquiring 1 signal at 50 Hz) were attached by trained researchers, connected to the Neuracle NeuroHUB wearable multimodal research platform, as shown in Fig. \ref{fig1}. Signal quality was checked after placement. The facial expression recording camera, a Logitech BRIO 500, was positioned on the top of the monitor used for stimulus viewing. 

\begin{figure}[htbp]   
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{Figures/Device.pdf}
    \caption{Neuracle NeuroHUB wearable acquisition device wearing method and EEG electrode positions.}
    \label{fig1}
\end{figure}

The overall experimental procedure is illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig2}. The experiment consisted of three separate sessions conducted on different days, with at least a 24-hour interval between sessions. Each session comprised 30 trials, presenting 5 distinct videos for each of the 6 basic emotions. The presentation followed a fixed sequence of six emotion categories: Happiness $\rightarrow$ Surprise $\rightarrow$ Disgust $\rightarrow$ Anger $\rightarrow$ Fear $\rightarrow$ Sadness. This block was repeated five times within the session. For each repetition cycle, a unique video for the corresponding emotion category in the sequence was selected without replacement from the pool of five available videos for that category. This design ensured all 30 videos (5 per emotion) were presented exactly once per session while maintaining the fixed progression of emotion types.

\begin{figure*}[!ht]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=18 cm,height=10cm]{Figures/experiment_process.pdf}
	\caption{Experimental paradigm for FIRMED data collection, showing the multi-session design, the procedure within a single trial (including baseline, video stimulus presentation, immediate replay with recall-based discrete annotation, and rest), the multimodal physiological and behavioral signals recorded, and the dimensions of emotion annotation (label, intensity, time).}
	\label{fig2}
\end{figure*}
Each trial consisted of four phases:

(1) \textit{Baseline}: A fixation cross was displayed on the screen for 10 seconds. Participants were asked to relax and minimize movement. Physiological and behavioral data corresponding to this period were collected.

(2) \textit{Stimulus Presentation}: One of the about 1-minute emotion-eliciting video clips was presented. Participants were instructed to watch the video naturally and keep their bodies as still as possible. Physiological and facial data corresponding to this period were collected.

(3) \textit{Immediate Replay and Annotation}:  Immediately following stimulus presentation, the video was replayed. Participants recalled their emotional experience from the initial viewing and indicated to the experimenter when they first experienced the target emotion. Due to GSR and PPG sensors on their fingers preventing direct interface control, the experimenter operated the annotation software based on participant instructions. Using the interface controls shown in Fig. \ref{fig3}, including an adjustable progress bar, the experimenter navigated to the precise timestamp identified by the participant. Upon participant confirmation, the experimenter paused the replay and recorded the timestamp. \subsection{Data preprocessing}\label{section:sec3.4}

Prior to analysis, the continuously recorded raw multimodal signals underwent filtering to remove noise and artifacts by MNE-Python \cite{gramfort2014mne}. Specifically:

\textbf{EEG data}: The EEG signals were first downsampled to 250 Hz to reduce computational load while preserving relevant frequency information. The data were then band-pass filtered between 0.5 Hz and 70 Hz using a finite impulse response (FIR) filter, followed by a 50 Hz notch filter to remove power line noise. Independent Component Analysis (ICA) \cite{makeig1995independent} was employed to identify and remove typical artifacts including eye blinks (EOG) and muscle activity (EMG). Bad channels were identified using a variance-based criterion: channels with variance exceeding 10 times the median variance across all channels were marked as 'bad' and subsequently repaired using spherical spline interpolation.

\textbf{ECG data}: ECG signals were band-pass filtered between 0.5 Hz and 40 Hz using a 4th-order Butterworth filter to remove baseline wander and high-frequency noise.

\textbf{GSR data}: GSR signals were preprocessed primarily focusing on the tonic component. For this, a low-pass filter was applied with a cutoff frequency of 0.5 Hz.

\textbf{PPG data}: PPG signal were band-pass filtered between 0.5 Hz and 8 Hz using a 4th-order Butterworth filter to retain the primary pulse wave frequencies while removing baseline drift and noise.

Subsequently, analysis epochs were extracted based on the discrete event timestamps $t_{event}$ identified during the annotation phase. Acknowledging that $t_{event}$ represents a subjective recollection of emotion onset and thus likely contains temporal jitter (due to factors such as memory precision limitations, reaction time during annotation, and the inherent difficulty in pinpointing the exact onset of a subjective feeling), and considering that physiological responses typically unfold over a period rather than being instantaneous, we employed a fixed window approach for analysis. Specifically, for each annotated $t_{event}$, a 4-second window was extracted from the preprocessed multimodal data streams \cite{hajcak2010event}, encompassing 2 seconds before and 2 seconds after $t_{event}$ (i.e., [$t_{event} - 2\,\text{s}, t_{event} + 2\,\text{s}$]). This window duration was selected to capture the most salient physiological changes surrounding the reported emotional event while accommodating the potential temporal variability \cite{muhl2014survey}.

\section{Physiological Validation of the Annotation Paradigm}\label{section:sec4}
In Section \ref{section:sec3}, we detailed the experimental procedure, the novel annotation paradigm, and the preprocessing methods for the multimodal data. This Section presents in-depth analyses of the multimodal physiological signals based on the processed data, the corresponding annotations, and the time windows defined around the annotated events, aiming to physiologically validate the annotation effectiveness. The analysis comprises two main parts: first, the results of the EEG signal analysis in Section \ref{section:sec4.1}; second, the results of the peripheral physiological signal analysis in Section \ref{section:sec4.2}; and finally, Section \ref{section:sec4.3} quantitatively evaluates the comparative results of our immediate annotation paradigm relative to a delayed annotation paradigm.



\subsection{EEG Analysis Results}\label{section:sec4.1}

This subsection details the EEG analysis results aimed at identifying brain neural correlates associated with the precisely annotated emotional event markers $t_{event}$ derived from the FIRMED. We focused on event-related changes in Power Spectral Density (PSD), comparing activity within the emotion-event time windows to the pre-trial baseline period \cite{liu2017real}. PSD was chosen as it is a well-established method for quantifying the distribution of power across different frequency bands in EEG signals, providing insights into the neural oscillatory changes that are widely recognized as correlates of various cognitive and emotional states. We calculated the PSD for each channel across standard frequency bands: $\delta$ (1-4 Hz), $\theta$ (4-8 Hz), $\alpha$ (8-13 Hz), $\beta$ (13-30 Hz) and $\gamma$ (30-45 Hz). For each participant and trial, preprocessed EEG data were extracted for the emotion-event time windows and the 10s baseline window. PSD for each channel within each window was calculated using Welch's method. 


For each participant and emotion category, the difference change in PSD from baseline to the event window is shown in \eqref{eq:eq1}. Subsequently, to assess the statistical significance of these changes at the group level, one-sample t-tests were performed at each electrode location to test whether the group-averaged $\Delta PSD$ values differed significantly from zero. To address the multiple comparisons problem inherent in simultaneous testing across 59 EEG channels, we employed cluster-based permutation testing \cite{maris2007nonparametric}. This approach involves forming spatial clusters of electrodes showing consistent effects based on their adjacency relationships, followed by 1000 random permutations where the sign of each participant's $\Delta PSD$ values is randomly flipped to simulate the null hypothesis of no systematic effect. Cluster-level statistics (sum of t-values within each cluster) from the observed data are then compared against the distribution of maximum cluster statistics obtained from the permutations to determine statistical significance. This non-parametric statistical method effectively controls the family-wise error rate by taking into account the spatial dependencies between channels, thereby offering greater sensitivity to detect genuine, spatially coherent neural effects. The findings described below highlight patterns observed at the group level based on these average effects.
\begin{equation}
 \Delta PSD=PSD_{event}-PSD_{baseline}
 \label{eq:eq1}
\end{equation}

This extensive $\gamma$ enhancement, particularly prominent in frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions, supports the neural binding hypothesis and suggests widespread cross-regional integration during positive emotional experiences \cite{muller1999processing}. The $\beta$ band exhibited a selective activation pattern involving 27 electrodes (45.8\%) organized into two distinct clusters ($p = 0.018$ and $p = 0.001$, $d = -0.46$ to $1.17$). where $e$ represents a specific emotion category, $n$ is the total number of subjects, $m_i$ is the total number of emotion $e$ events experienced by the $i$-th participant, $\overline{m}$ is the average number of emotion $e$ events per participant $I(SCR_{ij}(e) > 0.05\mu S)$ is an indicator function, equal to 1 when the SCR amplitude of the $i$-th participant's $j$-th emotion $e$ event within 2 seconds exceeds the threshold of 0.05$\mu$S, and 0 otherwise $SCR_{ij}(e)$ represents the maximum SCR amplitude of the $i$-th participant during the 2 seconds following the $j$-th emotion $e$ event.

\subsection{Comparative of Immediate versus Delayed Recall Annotation Paradigms}\label{section:sec4.3}

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed annotation approach, we conducted a controlled comparative experiment examining the differences between immediate and delayed recall annotation methods.  The study employed a within-participant design with the same 20 participants from the FIRMED. We selected 48 videos from the SEED-VII dataset as stimuli, comprising 8 videos for each of the six basic emotions. The experimental protocol was carefully balanced: the first 24 videos utilized the immediate recall annotation paradigm (as in FIRMED), while the remaining 24 videos employed the delayed recall approach (as in SEED-VII). This design allowed us to assess the impact of memory bias on annotation quality through both subjective and objective measures.

First, participants rated their subjective confidence regarding annotation accuracy using a 7-point Likert scale (1 = completely unsure, 7 = extremely certain) \cite{joshi2015likert}. Descriptive statistics indicated that the mean confidence in the immediate annotation condition (Mean = 6.85, SD = 0.21) was numerically higher than in the delayed condition (Mean = 5.91, SD = 1.35). Crucially, there was a significant difference in response variability between the conditions. A Levene's test \cite{schultz1985levene} was conducted to statistically evaluate the equality of variances, revealing significant heterogeneity (F(1, 38) = 47.2, $p$ \textless 0.001). To further quantify this relative dispersion, we computed the coefficient of variation (CV) \cite{abdi2010coefficient}, which calculated as CV = SD/Mean. The CV for the immediate condition was only 3.1\%, substantially lower than the delayed condition’s 22.8\%. This suggests that the delayed annotation significantly increased annotation inconsistency and uncertainty.

Second, building on our findings from Section \ref{section:sec4.2}, which established the SCR as a robust physiological marker of high-arousal emotions, we quantitatively evaluated the temporal concordance between annotated events and autonomic activation. We calculated the probability of valid SCR occurrence within a 4-second window at the annotated event. The results demonstrated that the SCR concordance probability under the immediate annotation paradigm is 76.3\%  higher than the delayed paradigm 69.7\%. This numerical trend aligns with the subjective confidence results, suggesting that the delayed annotation paradigm may impair temporal alignment between labels and actual physiological response peaks. The converging evidence from both subjective confidence ratings and objective physiological concordance robustly supports the efficacy of the immediate replay discrete annotation paradigm in mitigating memory bias and enhancing label accuracy. 

The analyses presented in this section provide multifaceted validation for our proposed annotation paradigm. First, through internal physiological validation, we established a strong temporal correspondence between the discrete annotation points within the FIRMED dataset and objective physiological signatures, spanning both emotion-specific neural oscillations and autonomic arousal indexed by SCRs. Furthermore, a comparative experiment demonstrated the superiority of our immediate annotation method over the traditional delayed approach in mitigating key indicators of memory bias, namely subjective uncertainty and response variability. Collectively, these findings confirm that the proposed paradigm offers a foundational solution to the challenge of label noise in emotion research by addressing the issue at the point of data annotation, rather than through subsequent, post-hoc corrections.

\section{Impact of Annotation on Emotion Recognition}\label{section:sec5}
This section presents a computational analysis to determine if our precise annotation paradigm yields superior emotion recognition performance. To isolate the impact of annotation quality, we conducted a rigorously controlled experiment. We created two datasets from the identical underlying physiological recordings: FIRMED, which uses our precise, recall-based annotations, and a control dataset, FIRMED-Whole, which applies traditional whole-trial labeling. By keeping all other experimental factors—such as feature extraction, classification models, and cross-validation procedures—identical across both conditions, this comparative framework allows any resulting performance differences to be robustly attributed to the annotation strategy itself.

\subsection{Dataset Construction}

In order to achieve comparative experiments, this study constructed two datasets as follows:

\textbf{FIRMED}: For this dataset, we implemented a conservative data augmentation strategy that follows the temporal precision of our annotations while acknowledging the inherent uncertainty in emotion onset timing. For each annotated emotional event at time  $t_{event}$, we extracted three overlapping 4-second windows: the primary window centered at  $t_{event}$ ([ $t_{event}$ - 2s,  $t_{event}$ + 2s]), and two adjacent windows shifted by ±1 second ([ $t_{event}$ - 3s,  $t_{event}$ + 1s] and [ $t_{event}$ - 1s,  $t_{event}$ + 3s]). This approach ensures that each window maintains substantial overlap with the annotated event time, preserving the temporal precision that distinguishes our annotation paradigm while providing modest data augmentation. All windows derived from the same emotional event inherited the original emotion label.


\textbf{FIRMED-Whole}: To simulate traditional whole-trial annotation, we used the entire physiological recording during the presentation of each video stimulus as described in Section \ref{section:sec3.3}. This entire about 1-minute segment was assigned the single emotion label reported by the participant at the timestamp within that video. For the FIRMED-Whole dataset, to maintain consistency in segment length with FIRMED for feature extraction and model input, and also to increase the sample size, we also performed overlapping 4-second window segmentation on whole data, with a step of 2-second. 
\subsection{Feature Extraction}\label{sec:sec5.2}
For all generated 4-second data segments in both the FIRMED and FIRMED-Whole datasets, we extracted the following features from the preprocessed data:

For EEG data, we selected Differential Entropy (DE) \cite{duan2013differential}, a feature well-established for its efficacy in capturing the complex, non-linear dynamics of neural oscillations in emotion recognition. Specifically, DE was computed for each of the 59 EEG channels across five standard frequency bands, resulting in a 295-dimensional feature vector (59 channels × 5 bands) for each 4-second segment. The calculation method is shown in equation \eqref{eq:eq3}:

\begin{equation}
DE = \frac{1}{2} \log(2 \pi e \sigma^2) 
\label{eq:eq3}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma^2$  is the variance of the signal in each frequency band, obtained via bandpass filtering.

From the GSR data, we extracted the skewness of its first derivative \eqref{eq:eq4}, a choice motivated by its ability to precisely quantify the rapid, phasic increases in skin conductance that our physiological analysis identified as a hallmark of high-arousal emotions \cite{kipli2022gsr}.
\begin{equation}
Skewness = \frac{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(v_i - \mu_v\right)^3}{\sigma_v^3}
\label{eq:eq4}
\end{equation}
where $v_i$ denotes the GSR derivative at time point $i$, representing the instantaneous rate of change in skin conductance. $N$ is the total number of samples within the 4-second analysis window. $\mu_v$ represents the mean of all derivative values across the window, indicating the average trend of GSR change. $\sigma_v$ is the standard deviation of the derivative values, measuring the variability of GSR change rates throughout the window.

From ECG data, we computed Root Mean Square of Successive Differences (RMSSD) \cite{berntson2005filter} to quantify short-term heart rate variability:
\begin{equation}
RMSSD = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (RR_{i+1} - RR_i)^2}
\label{eq:eq5}
\end{equation}
where $RR_i$ represents the $i$-th R-R interval in seconds, and $N$ is the total number of R-R intervals within the 4-second window. This metric is particularly sensitive to parasympathetic nervous system activity, with lower values indicating sympathetic dominance during high-arousal states and higher values reflecting parasympathetic influence in calm states.

From PPG data, we calculated the change rate of Pulse Wave Amplitude (PWA) \cite{proencca2019pulse} to capture peripheral vascular dynamics:
\begin{equation}
{PWA}_i = {PPG}_{{peak},i} - {PPG}_{{valley},i}
\label{eq:eq6}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\Delta PWA = \frac{\overline{PWA}_{post} - \overline{PWA}_{pre}}{\overline{PWA}_{total}}
\label{eq:eq7}
\end{equation}

where ${PPG}_{{peak},i}$ and $PPG_{valley,i}$ represent the systolic peak and diastolic valley of the $i$-th pulse wave, respectively. $\overline{PWA}_{{pre}}$ and $\overline{PWA}_{post}$ denote the mean amplitudes in the first and second halves of the window, while $\overline{PWA}_{total}$ is the overall mean. This feature detects emotion-induced vasoconstriction  or vasodilation.

\subsection{Classification Results and Analysis}

\subsubsection{EEG-based Emotion Recognition}

To comprehensively evaluate the impact of annotation precision on emotion recognition performance, we employed multiple classification algorithms spanning machine learning and deep learning approaches. We selected eight EEG-based representative classifiers to ensure our findings are robust across different algorithmic, as follows:

\textbf{Support Vector Machine (SVM)} \cite{wang2011eeg}: RBF kernel with hyperparameters optimized via grid search ($C \in {0.1, 1, 10, 100}$, $\gamma \in {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}$)

\textbf{k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)} \cite{li2018emotion}: k=5, using Euclidean distance metric.

\textbf{Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)} \cite{riedmiller2014multi}: Three hidden layers (128, 64, 32 neurons) with ReLU activation and dropout (0.3).

\textbf{EEGNet} \cite{lawhern2018eegnet}: A compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture specifically designed for EEG signals, effectively employing depthwise separable convolutions to learn spatio-temporal features..

\textbf{Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)} \cite{graves2012long}: A two-layer stacked LSTM architecture was used to capture temporal dependencies within the EEG sequences.

\textbf{Dynamic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (DGCNN)} \cite{song2018eeg}: A graph neural network variant where the graph's adjacency matrix is treated as learnable parameters, allowing for dynamic capture of inter-channel relationships.

\textbf{Multi-domain Dynamic Graph Representation Learning (MD$^2$GRL)} \cite{tang2024multi}: A method designed for learning dynamic graph representations from EEG by simultaneously leveraging features from both time and frequency domains.

\textbf{Transformer} \cite{vaswani2017attention}: Self-attention based model adapted for EEG sequences with positional encoding and 4 attention heads.

To assess cross-subject generalization, we used a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation scheme. For each of the 20 participants, the model was trained on the other 19 and tested on the held-out individual. Final performance metrics were then averaged across all 20 test results.

The analysis of these results yields several key insights. First, the superior performance of graph-based models DGCNN and MD$^2$GRL validates the importance of capturing inter-channel relationships in EEG data. Second, universal performance gains were observed across all algorithms, highlighting the algorithm-agnostic benefit of high-precision annotation. Furthermore, the performance delta between traditional and deep learning approaches widened on the FIRMED dataset, indicating that high-quality labels are crucial for complex models to learn robust and meaningful patterns. Finally, the highest classification accuracies were achieved for "Fear" and "Happiness," a finding that directly corroborates our conclusion from the physiological analysis that these two emotions have the most unique neural signal signatures.

\subsubsection{Multimodal Emotion Recognition}

Given that the DGCNN demonstrated superior performance among the evaluated models in the EEG-based emotion recognition tasks, it was selected as the primary architecture for a detailed exploration of multimodal fusion. To effectively integrate features derived from peripheral physiological signals (GSR, ECG, PPG) with the graph-based representations learned from EEG data by the DGCNN, we adopted a feature-level fusion strategy. This approach allows each data modality to be processed by an architecture best suited to its inherent structure before their learned representations are combined for final classification. 

The multimodal DGCNN architecture was conceptualized with two primary processing streams, the outputs of which were combined differently depending on the specific modality combination under evaluation, as presented in Table \ref{tab:modality_combinations_performance}.

The EEG data, these graph convolutional layers from DGCNN are designed to extract high-level feature embeddings that capture both channel-specific activities and complex spatio-temporal dependencies. The output from this stream, subsequent to the graph convolution and any graph pooling operations, is a flattened feature vector $F_{EEG}$ representing the learned EEG-specific information. For each specific multimodal combination to be evaluated, a feature vector was constructed using only the features from the peripheral signal(s) pertinent to that combination (Skewness, RMSSD, $\Delta$PWA, as defined in Section \ref{sec:sec5.2}). This tailored peripheral feature vector was then processed through a MLP sub-network, consisting of one dense layer with a non-linear activation function, to yield an abstract peripheral feature representation, denoted as $F_{Peripheral}$.

In all multimodal scenarios, the learned EEG feature vector $F_{EEG}$ was concatenated with the corresponding abstract peripheral feature vector $F_{Peripheral}$, which represented the specific peripheral signal(s) chosen for that particular test combination. This comprehensive vector was then fed into identical final fully-connected layers, culminating in a softmax layer, for predicting the target emotional states.

The results for the DGCNN model, presented in Table \ref{tab:modality_combinations_performance}, unequivocally demonstrate the benefits of integrating peripheral physiological signals with EEG data for emotion recognition. All tested multimodal combinations surpassed the EEG-only baseline performance on both FIRMED and FIRMED-Whole datasets. Notably, the comprehensive fusion of EEG with all peripheral signals yielded the highest accuracy, achieving 69.5\% on the FIRMED dataset. Among the single peripheral additions, EEG+GSR provided the most substantial improvement over EEG-only, reaching an accuracy of 67.0\%, underscoring GSR's strong capability in capturing arousal-related emotional dynamic.

Critically, the advantage of precise temporal annotation remained consistent and significant across all multimodal configurations. For every combination, models trained on the FIRMED dataset achieved superior accuracy compared to those trained on FIRMED-Whole; for example, the full multimodal accuracy on FIRMED was 6.0\% higher than its counterpart on FIRMED-Whole. This robustly illustrates that the enhanced data quality derived from our precise annotation paradigm effectively synergizes with the richer information from combined physiological signals, leading to optimal emotion recognition performance and further validating the overall dataset construction and annotation methodology.

\section{Conclusion}\label{section:sec6}

To address the prevalent challenges of label noise in video-induced emotion datasets, this paper introduces FIRMED, a multimodal dataset developed using an immediate recall-based annotation paradigm. Our comprehensive validation demonstrates the paradigm's methodological rigor and empirical effectiveness across multiple analytical dimensions.

Physiologically, we established temporal alignment between participant-reported emotional events and objective neurophysiological signatures, including emotion-specific oscillatory patterns across EEG frequency bands and distinctive autonomic activation profiles. This provides validation of the subjective-objective correspondence that has long been theoretically postulated but rarely systematically verified in emotion research. Computationally, classification models trained on precisely annotated data demonstrated consistent and substantial performance improvements across eight distinct algorithms, and multimodal approaches demonstrated superior performance compared to EEG-only configurations. These computational findings align with conclusions from SEED-VII \cite{jiang2024seed}, reinforcing that annotation quality serves as a critical determinant of recognition performance.

We acknowledge several limitations that warrant consideration. The dataset scale constrains statistical power and generalizability across diverse populations. The fixed 4-second analysis window, while physiologically informed, may not optimally capture the heterogeneous temporal dynamics of emotional responses across individuals and emotional contexts. Future investigations should prioritize expanding participant diversity across demographics, implementing adaptive temporal windowing techniques that accommodate individual response variability.

title: Accelerating Computation of Stable Merge Tree Edit Distances using Parameterized Heuristics
summary:
In this paper, we present a novel heuristic algorithm for the stable but
NP-complete deformation-based edit distance on merge trees. Our key
contribution is the introduction of a user-controlled look-ahead parameter that
allows to trade off accuracy and computational cost. We achieve a fixed
parameter tractable running time that is polynomial in the size of the input
but exponential in the look-ahead value. This extension unlocks the potential
of the deformation-based edit distance in handling saddle swaps, while
maintaining feasible computation times. Experimental results demonstrate the
computational efficiency and effectiveness of this approach in handling
specific perturbations.

bib.abstract: A new graphical display is proposed for partitioning techniques. Each cluster is represented by a so-called silhouette, which is based on the comparison of its tightness and separation. The entire clustering is displayed by combining the silhouettes into a single plot, allowing an appreciation of the relative quality of the clusters and an overview of the data configuration. The average silhouette width provides an evaluation of clustering validity, and might be used to select an ‘appropriate’ number of clusters.

bib.abstract:
Characteristic curves of vector fields include stream, path, and streak
lines. Stream and path lines can be obtained by a simple vector field
integration of an autonomous ODE system, i.e., they can be described
as tangent curves of a vector field. This facilitates their mathematical
analysis including the extraction of core lines around which stream
or path lines exhibit swirling motion, or the computation of their
curvature for every point in the domain without actually integrating
them. Such a description of streak lines is not yet available, which
excludes them from most of the feature extraction and analysis tools
that have been developed in our community. In this paper, we develop
the first description of streak lines as tangent curves of a derived
vector field -- the streak line vector field -- and show how it can
be computed from the spatial and temporal gradients of the flow map,
i.e., a dense path line integration is required. We demonstrate the
high accuracy of our approach by comparing it to solutions where
the ground truth is analytically known and to solutions where the
ground truth has been obtained using the classic streak line computation.
Furthermore, we apply a number of feature extraction and analysis
tools to the new streak line vector field including the extraction
of cores of swirling streak lines and the computation of streak line
curvature fields. These first applications foreshadow the large variety
of possible future research directions based on our new mathematical
description of streak lines.

title: Global Profits, Local Decisions: Why Global Cooperation Falters in Multi-level Games
summary:
Global cooperation often falters despite shared objectives, as misaligned
interests and unequal incentives undermine collective efforts, such as those in
international climate change collaborations. To tackle this issue, this paper
introduces a multi-level game-theoretic model to analyze the dynamics of
complex interactions within hierarchical systems. The model consists of global,
local, and pairwise games, and two strategy types, binary and level-based
strategies, are explored under varying parameter conditions. Using
computational simulations and numerical analysis, we examine how factors across
different levels influence player decisions, game dynamics and population phase
transitions during the evolutionary process. Our findings reveal that although
the increase of profit rates at local and pairwise games enhances cooperation
within the population, the global game exerts minimal influence on player
decisions and population states under both strategy settings. Particularly,
analytical and simulation results show that, under binary strategies, global
profit does not influence localized decision-making of players, while under
level-based strategies, players cooperating at the global level are eventually
outcompeted due to the evolutionary disadvantage even when global profit is
substantial. These insights contribute to a theoretical understanding of
cooperation dynamics in multi-level systems and may offer implications for
fostering global collaboration on challenges like climate change.

title: An approach for modularly verifying the core of Rust's atomic reference counting algorithm against the (X)C20 memory consistency model
summary:
We propose an approach for modular verification of programs that use
relaxed-consistency atomic memory access primitives and fences, sufficient for
verifying the core of Rust's Atomic Reference Counting (ARC) algorithm, and we
argue its soundness, when combined with a simple static analysis and admitting
an open sub-problem, with respect to the C20 memory consistency model, as well
as, even in the absence of any static analysis and without any assumptions,
with respect to XC20, a recently proposed minor strengthening of C20 that rules
out out-of-thin-air behaviors but allows load buffering. In contrast to
existing work on verifying ARC, we do not assume acyclicity of the union of the
program-order and reads-from relations. We define an interleaving operational
semantics, prove its soundness with respect to (X)C20's axiomatic semantics,
and then apply any existing program logic for fine-grained interleaving
concurrency, such as Iris.

title: Quantum-Assisted Machine Learning Models for Enhanced Weather Prediction
summary:
Quantum Machine Learning (QML) presents as a revolutionary approach to
weather forecasting by using quantum computing to improve predictive modeling
capabilities. In this study, we apply QML models, including Quantum Gated
Recurrent Units (QGRUs), Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), Quantum Long
Short-Term Memory(QLSTM), Variational Quantum Circuits(VQCs), and Quantum
Support Vector Machines(QSVMs), to analyze meteorological time-series data from
the ERA5 dataset. Our methodology includes preprocessing meteorological
features, implementing QML architectures for both classification and regression
tasks. The results demonstrate that QML models can achieve reasonable accuracy
in both prediction and classification tasks, particularly in binary
classification. However, challenges such as quantum hardware limitations and
noise affect scalability and generalization. This research provides insights
into the feasibility of QML for weather prediction, paving the way for further
exploration of hybrid quantum-classical frameworks to enhance meteorological
forecasting.

bib.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning on quantum computers have been made possible mainly by two discoveries. Mapping the features into exponentially large Hilbert spaces makes them linearly separable---quantum circuits perform linear operations only. The parameter-shift rule allows for easy computation of objective function gradients on quantum hardware---a classical optimizer can then be used to find its minimum. This allows us to build a binary variational quantum classifier that shows some advantages over the classical one. In this paper we extend this idea to building a multi-class classifier and apply it to real data. A systematic study involving several feature maps and classical optimizers as well as different repetitions of the parametrized circuits is presented. The accuracy of the model is compared both on a simulated environment and on a real IBM quantum computer.

bib.abstract: Accurate solar power forecasting is pivotal for the global transition towards sustainable energy systems. This study conducts a meticulous comparison between Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) and classical Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models for solar power production forecasting. The primary objective is to evaluate the potential advantages of QLSTMs, leveraging their exponential representational capabilities, in capturing the intricate spatiotemporal patterns inherent in renewable energy data. Through controlled experiments on real-world photovoltaic datasets, our findings reveal promising improvements offered by QLSTMs, including accelerated training convergence and substantially reduced test loss within the initial epoch compared to classical LSTMs. These empirical results demonstrate QLSTM’s potential to swiftly assimilate complex time series relationships, enabled by quantum phenomena like superposition. However, realizing QLSTM’s full capabilities necessitates further research into model validation across diverse conditions, systematic hyperparameter optimization, hardware noise resilience, and applications to correlated renewable forecasting problems. With continued progress, quantum machine learning can offer a paradigm shift in renewable energy time series prediction, potentially ushering in an era of unprecedented accuracy and reliability in solar power forecasting worldwide. This pioneering work provides initial evidence substantiating quantum advantages over classical LSTM models while acknowledging present limitations. Through rigorous benchmarking grounded in real-world data, our study illustrates a promising trajectory for quantum learning in renewable forecasting.

bib.abstract: Abstract Within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), ECMWF is producing the ERA5 reanalysis which, once completed, will embody a detailed record of the global atmosphere, land surface and ocean waves from 1950 onwards. This new reanalysis replaces the ERA-Interim reanalysis (spanning 1979 onwards) which was started in 2006. ERA5 is based on the Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) Cy41r2 which was operational in 2016. ERA5 thus benefits from a decade of developments in model physics, core dynamics and data assimilation. In addition to a significantly enhanced horizontal resolution of 31 km, compared to 80 km for ERA-Interim, ERA5 has hourly output throughout, and an uncertainty estimate from an ensemble (3-hourly at half the horizontal resolution). This paper describes the general set-up of ERA5, as well as a basic evaluation of characteristics and performance, with a focus on the dataset from 1979 onwards which is currently publicly available. Re-forecasts from ERA5 analyses show a gain of up to one day in skill with respect to ERA-Interim. Comparison with radiosonde and PILOT data prior to assimilation shows an improved fit for temperature, wind and humidity in the troposphere, but not the stratosphere. A comparison with independent buoy data shows a much improved fit for ocean wave height. The uncertainty estimate reflects the evolution of the observing systems used in ERA5. The enhanced temporal and spatial resolution allows for a detailed evolution of weather systems. For precipitation, global-mean correlation with monthly-mean GPCP data is increased from 67\% to 77\%. In general, low-frequency variability is found to be well represented and from 10 hPa downwards general patterns of anomalies in temperature match those from the ERA-Interim, MERRA-2 and JRA-55 reanalyses.

bib.abstract: In this paper, we performed an analysis of the 500 most relevant scientific articles published since 2018, concerning machine learning methods in the field of climate and numerical weather prediction using the Google Scholar search engine. The most common topics of interest in the abstracts were identified, and some of them examined in detail: in numerical weather prediction research—photovoltaic and wind energy, atmospheric physics and processes; in climate research—parametrizations, extreme events, and climate change. With the created database, it was also possible to extract the most commonly examined meteorological fields (wind, precipitation, temperature, pressure, and radiation), methods (Deep Learning, Random Forest, Artificial Neural Networks, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost), and countries (China, USA, Australia, India, and Germany) in these topics. Performing critical reviews of the literature, authors are trying to predict the future research direction of these fields, with the main conclusion being that machine learning methods will be a key feature in future weather forecasting.
